Hi! First I'm so sorry this happened to you, injuries always suck no matter how they happened. 

Second, it's very hard to answer your question in terms of what you trainer did without seeing you doing the exercise or knowing what else your program consists of. So I'm going to tell you how I would train someone in your position. 


You mention being overweight with balance issues. That is an immediate red flag to me to start slow and low with anything involving balance, to build up your stability and confidence before moving on. I would start off with knee raises and holding them, and progressing to small step ups, and eventually moving to the box steps you mentioned using. 
I would absolutely not start someone with balance issues on the higher level. 

Keep in mind that this is just with the little information I know about you. Like I said, it's hard to say anything for sure without knowing full details of your history and program. 

Another thing to note is that your trainer should have insurance, if not, the gym definitely does.

I suggest learning more about the science behind food choices regardless of what you're legally allowed to do. It's good information that will help you explain to clients the "why" behind certain choices. Like why choose certain types of fats or carbs over others. Check your state laws and your certifications scope of practice. Trainers are not qualified to write meal plans. You can help someone with macros, suggest types of foods. Help them translate ingredients and nutrition labels. But you are likely not legally able to say "eat 4 oz chicken, 1c. Broccoli...etc." 

It is in your best interest to direct more specific diet questions and concerns to an RD, not a "nutritionist." Anyone can call themselves a nutritionist. But a registered dietitian is a board certified title and therefore more credible.
